entry.title: Making sure AI chips don’t overheat in space

media:group.media:title: Making sure AI chips don’t overheat in space
media:group.media:description:
Project Suncatcher is Google’s moonshot to launch solar-powered AI into Earth’s orbit. But operating TPU clusters in space creates a massive hurdle.
On Earth, cooling chips means blowing air over heat sinks. In the vacuum of space, there is no air.
In this video, Google researchers share the thermal engineering challenge of moving heat, using heat pipes, pumped fluid loops, and thermal vacuum chambers.
00:10 - How do we cool AI chips in space? 01:05 - How do heat pipes and fluid loops move heat to radiators? 01:26 - How do thermal vacuum chambers simulate space on Earth?

entry.title: Keeping flying satellites connected with lasers

media:group.media:title: Keeping flying satellites connected with lasers
media:group.media:description:
To make space-based AI work, thousands of chips must communicate across a vacuum orbit with minimal delay, orbiting in a highly connected constellation.
Without physical cables, we use lasers fired between satellites to transfer information; the equivalent of hitting a moving, coin-sized target from kilometers away, over and over again.
In this video, Google researchers explain how they achieved an 800 Gbps bidirectional laser link by adapting off-the-shelf fiber optics.
00:15 - How can we keep the constellation connected? 00:38 - Why use lasers for satellite communication? 01:31 - Can terrestrial hardware work in space?

media:group.media:description:

In this video, the Project Suncatcher team tackles hardware survival: how do you build systems that can withstand 5 years of cosmic radiation, solar events, and the force of a rocket launch that generates acceleration loads up to 10 times the force of gravity?

entry.title: Google’s latest moonshot to put machine learning in space

media:group.media:title: Google’s latest moonshot to put machine learning in space
media:group.media:description:
A solar panel in space generates up to 8 times more power than one on Earth.
That’s the vision behind Project Suncatcher: Google’s moonshot to capture continuous sunlight and more efficiently power machine learning in space.
In this video, we explore some of the monumental engineering questions that must be answered to make this idea a reality.
0:14 - How do we put machine learning in space? 0:30 - How much power can solar panels generate in orbit? 0:55 - How do TPU satellites communicate? 1:40 - What is the future of space-based compute?
